context: Watson and Crick's 1953 paper proposed DNA as a double helix — two strands of sugar-phosphate backbone wound around each other, with paired bases (A-T, G-C) holding the strands together like rungs of a ladder. The structure suggested the copying mechanism: separate the strands and each serves as a template. Their model was built on X-ray diffraction data from Rosalind Franklin's lab. The Nature paper was just one page long but reshaped biology. Watson, Crick, and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel; Franklin had died of ovarian cancer in 1958.

question: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction work at King's College London was crucial to Watson and Crick's discovery of DNA's structure. One of her images, taken by her student Raymond Gosling, was especially decisive. What is it called?
answer: Photo 51, an X-ray diffraction image of DNA fibers
choices: Photo 51, an X-ray diffraction image of DNA fibers
The First X-Ray, the world's first medical X-ray image
The DNA Snapshot, a photograph taken with a regular camera
Diagram 51, a hand-drawn schematic of DNA's structure
context: Photo 51 was taken in May 1952 by Raymond Gosling under Franklin's direction. It showed an X-shaped diffraction pattern that revealed DNA's helical structure and key dimensions. In January 1953, Maurice Wilkins (Franklin's colleague but uneasy rival) showed the photo to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge — a move many consider ethically dubious. Watson and Crick built their model partly using Photo 51's data. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at age 37. The 1962 Nobel went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins; Nobel rules exclude posthumous awards.

question: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in TWO different sciences during her lifetime — the only person ever to do so. What were the two sciences?
answer: Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911)
choices: Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911)
Medicine (1905) and Chemistry (1920)
Physics (1903) and Medicine (1925)
Chemistry (1908) and Mathematics (1918)
context: Marie Curie (1867-1934) won the 1903 Physics Nobel (shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel) for research on radioactivity. She won the 1911 Chemistry Nobel (alone) for isolating polonium and radium. She remains the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences. Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also won a Nobel (Chemistry, 1935). Marie Curie died in 1934 from aplastic anemia, almost certainly caused by years of radiation exposure — the dangers were not understood at the time.

question: Marie and Pierre Curie isolated radium in 1902 after years of processing tons of pitchblende ore in a leaky shed in Paris. What did the pure radium DO that made it so striking?
answer: It glowed faintly in the dark, visible without any other light source
choices: It glowed faintly in the dark, visible without any other light source
It burst into flames the moment it was touched by sunlight
It was perfectly transparent, completely invisible to human eyes
It exploded when it touched any other metal whatsoever
context: Pure radium chloride glows faintly blue-green in the dark, energized by its own radioactive decay. The Curies often described their lab at night, with radium-containing vials emitting a soft glow on the shelves. The phenomenon enchanted Marie Curie and helped popularize radioactivity. Tragically, the glow's beauty obscured the danger — Marie Curie carried test tubes in her pockets and stored them on her bedside table. Her papers and personal effects remain too radioactive to handle without protection a century later.

question: Marie Curie named one of the two new elements she discovered after the country she came from. Which element honors her homeland?
answer: Polonium, named after her homeland of Poland
choices: Polonium, named after her homeland of Poland
Francium, named after France where she worked at the Sorbonne
Americium, named after America where her funding came from
Lithuanium, named after Lithuania where she grew up as a child
context: Marie Curie was born Maria Sklodowska in Warsaw in 1867, when Poland was partitioned and not an independent country. She moved to Paris in 1891 to study at the Sorbonne. In 1898 she and Pierre Curie discovered two new radioactive elements; she named the first 'polonium' after her homeland Poland, hoping to draw attention to its plight under foreign rule. The second they named radium for its intense radioactivity. Marie became a French citizen but kept her Polish patriotism throughout her life.

question: Norman Borlaug developed dwarf wheat varieties resistant to rust disease, helping triple harvests in Mexico, India, and Pakistan from the 1940s through the 1960s. What Nobel did he win?
answer: The Nobel Peace Prize in 1970
choices: The Nobel Peace Prize in 1970
The Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1965
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960
The Nobel Prize in Physics in 1955
context: Borlaug (1914-2009) won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for his agricultural work, which is credited with saving roughly one billion lives by averting predicted famines. His dwarf wheat varieties were short-stalked (so heads of grain wouldn't topple), highly responsive to fertilizer, and resistant to multiple rust diseases. The 'Green Revolution' transformed agriculture in the developing world. Borlaug worked into his nineties pushing for African agricultural reform, and was outspoken against organic-only food orthodoxy in poor countries that he saw as a luxury that would cost lives.

question: Tu Youyou is a Chinese pharmaceutical chemist who discovered an effective antimalarial drug by reading ancient Chinese medical texts during the 1960s-70s. What is the drug, and when did she win her Nobel?
answer: Artemisinin, derived from sweet wormwood; she won the Nobel in 2015
choices: Artemisinin, derived from sweet wormwood; she won the Nobel in 2015
Penicillin, derived from mold; she won the Nobel in 1990
Aspirin, derived from willow bark; she won the Nobel in 2000
Quinine, derived from cinchona bark; she won the Nobel in 1980
context: Tu Youyou (born 1930) led 'Project 523,' a Chinese military program to find new malaria treatments during the Vietnam War. She and her team screened over 2,000 traditional Chinese remedies. A passage in a 4th-century text by Ge Hong led her to sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) and the active compound artemisinin. Tu tested it on herself first. Artemisinin-based combination therapies now save hundreds of thousands of lives a year. Tu won the 2015 Nobel in Physiology or Medicine — the first Chinese woman to win a science Nobel.

question: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier developed a powerful gene-editing tool, working on a system that bacteria use as a defense against viruses. What is the tool, and when did they win their Nobel?
answer: CRISPR-Cas9, with the Nobel awarded to them in 2020
choices: CRISPR-Cas9, with the Nobel awarded to them in 2020
PCR (polymerase chain reaction), with the Nobel awarded in 1993
Recombinant DNA, with the Nobel awarded in 1980
Restriction enzymes, with the Nobel awarded in 1978
context: CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is part of a bacterial immune system that cuts viral DNA. Doudna (UC Berkeley) and Charpentier (then in Sweden) repurposed it in 2012 as a programmable gene-editing tool. They won the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry — making them the first all-female team to win a science Nobel. CRISPR has produced approved treatments: Casgevy (2023) for sickle cell disease, Luxturna for inherited blindness, Zolgensma for spinal muscular atrophy. The technology is also at the center of ethical debates about human germline editing.

question: Demis Hassabis led the Google DeepMind team that built AlphaFold, an AI system that predicts protein structures from amino acid sequences. What Nobel did Hassabis win in 2024?
answer: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry (shared with John Jumper and David Baker)
choices: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry (shared with John Jumper and David Baker)
The Nobel Prize in Physics, for the underlying neural network design
The Nobel Prize in Medicine, for predicting disease structures only
The Nobel Prize in Peace, for sharing the model openly with science
context: Demis Hassabis (born 1976) co-founded DeepMind in 2010, which Google acquired in 2014. AlphaFold solved a 50-year-old challenge in biology — predicting how a protein folds from its amino acid sequence — at near-experimental accuracy. The free AlphaFold database (~200 million predicted structures) has transformed structural biology. Hassabis shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel with John Jumper (DeepMind colleague) and David Baker (University of Washington, separate protein-design work). It was the first major AI-driven Nobel.

question: In 1927 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 8-1 in 'Buck v. Bell' that compulsory sterilization of people deemed 'feeble-minded' was constitutional. What unusual legal fact remains true of this decision?
answer: It has never been formally overturned by the Supreme Court
choices: It has never been formally overturned by the Supreme Court
It was overturned the same year by a unanimous ruling
It was never actually decided, remaining an open case
It was overturned in 1928 after one year of outcry
context: Buck v. Bell (1927) upheld Virginia's compulsory-sterilization law for people deemed mentally unfit. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote the majority opinion, including the notorious line 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough.' Carrie Buck's IQ testing was later shown to have been rigged for the case. While Buck v. Bell has been quietly disregarded in practice for decades, the Supreme Court has never formally overturned it. Subsequent cases (Skinner v. Oklahoma 1942) limited but didn't reverse it. The case is a touchstone for warnings about science deferring to state power.

question: Compulsory-sterilization laws targeting people deemed 'feeble-minded' first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century. Which state passed the FIRST such law?
answer: Indiana, in 1907, the first such law in the world
choices: Indiana, in 1907, the first such law in the world
California, in 1875, the same decade as American statehood
Vermont, in 1850, the first state to consider eugenic policy
Massachusetts, in 1920, the last state to consider such a law
context: Indiana's 1907 sterilization law was the first in the world. By 1937, 32 U.S. states had similar laws. California led in numbers — over 20,000 people were sterilized there by the 1960s, often without informed consent and disproportionately affecting non-white, immigrant, and poor populations. The American eugenics movement, well-funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller through institutions like the Cold Spring Harbor Eugenics Record Office, was the most successful in the world before WWII. Nazi Germany's T4 program explicitly modeled American precedent.

question: The basic shape of the scientific method involves a few key steps. Which is the most accurate sequence?
answer: Observe a phenomenon, form a hypothesis, test it with experiments, refine or reject the hypothesis
choices: Observe a phenomenon, form a hypothesis, test it with experiments, refine or reject the hypothesis
Form a strong personal opinion, then convince others to agree with it
Ask a famous scientist what is true, then teach the same answer to others
Pick a fashionable theory, then look only for evidence that supports it
context: The 'scientific method' described in textbooks is an idealization — real science is messier than the textbook sequence. But the basic shape (observe, hypothesize, test, refine) captures what distinguishes scientific from non-scientific reasoning. Real science also requires peer review, replication, and the willingness of researchers to update beliefs when evidence accumulates against them. Paul Feyerabend's 1975 book 'Against Method' famously argued there is no single scientific method — physics, biology, and astronomy each work differently. The shape is real even if no single recipe captures it.

question: Philosopher Karl Popper proposed in the 1930s that a key marker of scientific claims is whether they can be tested and potentially shown false. What is this property called?
answer: Falsifiability, the property of making predictions that could fail
choices: Falsifiability, the property of making predictions that could fail
Confirmability, the property of always being shown true in some test
Believability, the property of being widely accepted by experts at first
Theoretical interest, the property of being mathematically elegant only
context: Karl Popper (1902-1994) argued in 'The Logic of Scientific Discovery' (1934) that a theory's scientific status depends on falsifiability — whether it makes predictions that could fail. 'Einstein's theory predicts light will bend by 1.75 arcseconds during an eclipse' is falsifiable; 'consciousness manifests in mysterious ways' is not. Popper criticized Freud and Marx for making theories so flexible no observation could refute them. Modern philosophy of science has refined Popper's view (Quine, Lakatos, Kuhn), but falsifiability remains a useful first test for distinguishing science from pseudoscience.

question: The COVID-19 pandemic raised an unresolved question about the origin of SARS-CoV-2. By 2023, what was the assessment from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Energy?
answer: Both publicly favored a laboratory origin as the most likely source
choices: Both publicly favored a laboratory origin as the most likely source
Both publicly agreed the virus was created by space aliens
Both declined to investigate the question of origins at all
Both ruled out a lab origin completely and unanimously
context: The lab leak hypothesis — that SARS-CoV-2 escaped from a Wuhan laboratory rather than emerging naturally — was widely labeled 'conspiracy theory' in 2020-2021 by major news outlets and public health figures. By 2023 the FBI publicly assessed lab leak as the most likely origin (with moderate confidence), and the U.S. Department of Energy publicly leaned the same way (with low confidence). FOIA-released 'Proximal Origin' Slack messages showed the authors of the influential paper dismissing lab leak privately considered it plausible — even as they publicly called it implausible.

question: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet MMR-autism paper was partially retracted in 2004 and fully retracted in 2010. What's the more accurate accounting beyond 'fraud, case closed'?
answer: Real methodology problems — AND broader vaccine-safety questions remain legitimate independent of his case
choices: Real methodology problems — AND broader vaccine-safety questions remain legitimate independent of his case
Wakefield right on everything — paper now the gold standard for safety
Identical to other papers — the retraction was routine procedure
No safety conversation exists — and the Wakefield episode never occurred
context: Brian Deer's investigation (Sunday Times then BMJ 2011) documented patient-selection problems and undisclosed conflicts. The MMR-autism causal claim doesn't hold up in larger studies. Separately, Wakefield's GI observations have been replicated independently. The retraction is used as a discussion-ender to dismiss subsequent credentialed vaccine-safety inquiry; that's a separable move.

question: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming returned to his lab at St. Mary's Hospital in London after a vacation. What did he notice growing on a contaminated petri dish that changed medicine forever?
answer: A mold that had killed nearby bacteria, the source of the first antibiotic
choices: A mold that had killed nearby bacteria, the source of the first antibiotic
A new species of bacteria that ate plastic from his lab equipment
A new color of bacteria never seen in laboratories before
A virus that could only grow on certain types of stained glass
context: Fleming (1881-1955) noticed that a contaminating mold (later identified as Penicillium notatum) had cleared bacteria from the area around it on a petri dish. He named the active substance 'penicillin' and published in 1929 — but couldn't isolate it at useful scale. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford did the hard chemistry in 1940-41, and Norman Heatley scaled production. By D-Day 1944 mass-produced penicillin was saving Allied soldiers. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel in Medicine.

question: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin's antibacterial effect in 1928 but couldn't make practical medicine from it. Who eventually isolated and produced penicillin at scale during World War II?
answer: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford University in 1940-41
choices: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford University in 1940-41
Marie Curie's daughter Irene Joliot-Curie at the Pasteur Institute
Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr at Princeton during the war years
Robert Koch and Louis Pasteur at the German Institute of Health
context: Florey (Australian pathologist) and Chain (German-Jewish chemist, refugee from Nazi Germany) led the Oxford team that isolated penicillin in usable form by 1940. Norman Heatley designed the production process. By 1941 they could treat human patients. American companies (Pfizer, Merck) scaled production to industrial levels. Florey traveled to the US to convince the wartime government to invest. By D-Day 1944, enough penicillin was available to treat every Allied soldier needing it. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel.

question: Jonas Salk developed an effective polio vaccine using inactivated (killed) virus, tested in massive field trials in the early 1950s. What did Salk do regarding a patent for his vaccine?
answer: He refused to patent it, saying it belonged to the people
choices: He refused to patent it, saying it belonged to the people
He patented it and earned billions of dollars in royalties from sales
He sold the patent to a single drug company for one dollar quietly
He patented it but the patent was rejected by the U.S. courts
context: Jonas Salk (1914-1995) tested his polio vaccine on himself and his family before public trials. The 1954 field trial enrolled 1.8 million American children — the largest medical experiment ever conducted. Results announced April 12, 1955 showed the vaccine effective; church bells rang across America. When CBS journalist Edward R. Murrow asked Salk who owned the patent, Salk famously replied: 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Polio is now eradicated from most of the world.

question: Edward Jenner's 1796 cowpox experiment gets called 'the first vaccine.' What's the older worldwide history the label buries?
answer: Variolation — mild smallpox itself was used in China, Africa, India, Ottoman Turkey for centuries
choices: Variolation — mild smallpox itself was used in China, Africa, India, Ottoman Turkey for centuries
Universal first — Jenner was the very first human to think about disease prevention
Disease was unknown — Jenner discovered smallpox itself in 1796
All vaccines must use cowpox — Jenner's exact technique is unchanged today
context: Variolation (deliberately exposing healthy people to mild smallpox material) was widely practiced in China by the 16th century, in West Africa, India, and Ottoman Turkey before reaching Britain in 1721 via Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. Jenner's cowpox version was safer. The 'first vaccine' label hides both the older non-European tradition and the special-case nature of cowpox-for-smallpox.

question: In the 1860s French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that microorganisms cause fermentation and disease — overturning the older 'spontaneous generation' theory. What clever experimental device did he use to make his case?
answer: Swan-necked flasks that let air enter but trapped airborne particles
choices: Swan-necked flasks that let air enter but trapped airborne particles
Glass tubes shaped exactly like the letter Z, viewed from above
Heated copper basins that destroyed all gases above the broth
Sealed buckets buried underground for thirty days at a time
context: Pasteur's 1859 swan-neck flask experiment was elegant. He boiled broth in flasks with long, curved necks that let air in but trapped dust and microbes in the curve. The broth stayed sterile for months — no spontaneous generation. When he broke the neck, the broth was quickly contaminated. The experiment refuted spontaneous generation and supported germ theory. Pasteur went on to develop pasteurization (heat-treating to kill microbes), rabies vaccine, and improved anthrax vaccine. His work, with Robert Koch's, established germ theory.

question: British surgeon Joseph Lister revolutionized surgery in the 1860s by introducing antiseptic techniques based on Pasteur's germ theory. What was his most famous antiseptic chemical?
answer: Carbolic acid (phenol), used to sterilize instruments and wounds
choices: Carbolic acid (phenol), used to sterilize instruments and wounds
Hydrogen peroxide, only invented after Lister's lifetime
Bleach, the same chlorine solution used today in households
Pure alcohol, never used in medicine because of its toxicity
context: Joseph Lister (1827-1912), inspired by Pasteur's germ theory, began using carbolic acid (phenol) to sterilize surgical instruments, wounds, and operating rooms in 1865 at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary. Post-surgical infection rates fell dramatically. British surgeons resisted his innovations for years (Listerism was mocked initially), but American surgeons adopted them more quickly. The mouthwash brand Listerine was named in his honor. Lister's work, together with Pasteur's, ushered in the modern era of surgical medicine.

question: In November 1895 the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen accidentally discovered a new kind of penetrating radiation in his Würzburg lab. What did he call it, and what was the first famous image he took?
answer: X-rays — and the first image was of his wife's hand showing her bones
choices: X-rays — and the first image was of his wife's hand showing her bones
Y-rays — and the first image was of a fish from a nearby river
M-rays — and the first image was of a cathedral's stone walls
Z-rays — and the first image was of the Earth's underground caves
context: Röntgen (1845-1923) noticed a faint glow on a fluorescent screen while working with cathode-ray tubes covered in black cardboard. Investigating further, he found an unknown form of radiation that passed through paper, wood, and flesh but not bone or metal. He called it 'X' for unknown. His December 1895 photograph of his wife Bertha's hand (showing her bones and her wedding ring) was the first medical X-ray and electrified the world. Röntgen won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for the discovery.

question: William Harvey published in 1628 that blood circulates through the body, pumped by the heart — overturning a 1500-year-old medical consensus. What was the older view he refuted?
answer: That blood was made constantly by the liver and consumed by tissues
choices: That blood was made constantly by the liver and consumed by tissues
That blood was a single still puddle in the chest cavity all day
That blood was only formed when people slept at night each day
That blood was a magical substance with no physical existence at all
context: The older view came from Galen (2nd century AD) and dominated Western medicine for 1500 years: the liver continuously produced new blood, which the body then consumed in tissues. William Harvey (1578-1657) calculated that the heart pumps far more blood per hour than the liver could possibly produce — therefore blood must CIRCULATE, returning to the heart. His 1628 book 'De motu cordis' (On the Motion of the Heart) overturned Galenic medicine. Harvey's work shows that long-held consensus can be wrong, and that careful measurement can defeat ancient authority.

question: Antoine Lavoisier (1743-1794) overturned the old 'phlogiston theory' of burning by identifying the actual chemistry of combustion. What did Lavoisier name the gas that combines with burning materials?
answer: Oxygen, from Greek for 'acid-former'
choices: Oxygen, from Greek for 'acid-former'
Phlogiston, keeping the old chemical name as an honor
Nitrogen, mistakenly using a name later assigned to a different gas
Helium, naming it after the Sun for its bright flames
context: Phlogiston theory held that burning materials released a substance called 'phlogiston.' Lavoisier (in the 1770s-80s) showed that burning materials COMBINE with a gas (oxygen) from air, GAINING mass. He named oxygen from Greek 'oxys' (sharp/acid) + 'genes' (former) because he believed it formed all acids (a partial misunderstanding). Lavoisier also identified hydrogen, established the law of conservation of mass, and built modern chemical nomenclature. He was guillotined in 1794 during the French Revolution at age 50. The mathematician Lagrange said: 'It took only a moment to cause that head to fall, and a hundred years will not be sufficient to produce another like it.'

question: Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, arranging the known chemical elements by atomic weight in rows and columns. What striking feature of his table convinced chemists it was correct?
answer: Gaps that predicted undiscovered elements, all of which were later found
choices: Gaps that predicted undiscovered elements, all of which were later found
An exact alphabetical arrangement of every element by English name
Color-coded illustrations that made it easy for children to memorize
A list ordered by which element was most abundant on Earth's surface
context: Mendeleev (1834-1907) arranged elements by atomic weight and noticed periodic recurrences of chemical properties. To preserve the pattern, he left gaps for predicted-but-unknown elements — including specific predictions of their atomic weights, densities, and reactivity. Gallium (1875), scandium (1879), and germanium (1886) were all later discovered matching Mendeleev's predictions closely. The successful predictions convinced even skeptical chemists. Modern periodic tables order elements by atomic NUMBER (protons), not atomic weight — but Mendeleev's organizational insight remains intact.

question: Wegener was rejected for 50 years over continental drift; Semmelweis was institutionalized for showing hand-washing saves lives; Marshall was ridiculed over the H. pylori-ulcer link. What lesson do these cases teach?
answer: Scientific consensus has been wrong many times and can update
choices: Scientific consensus has been wrong many times and can update
Scientific consensus has always been right and never changes
Outsiders to science are always wrong about medical claims
Scientific debates are decided only by public votes citywide
context: Wegener (continental drift, 1912 rejected, 1960s vindicated), Semmelweis (hand-washing, 1847 mocked, posthumously vindicated), Marshall + Warren (H. pylori, 1980s ridiculed, 2005 Nobel) are three classic cases — and there are more (Lister antisepsis, Mendel ignored, plate tectonics). The pattern doesn't mean every fringe claim is right (most are wrong). It does mean appealing to consensus as the final answer is bad epistemology. Real science updates; the careful question isn't 'do experts agree?' but 'what does the evidence actually show?'

question: The 2015 Open Science Collaboration tried to redo 100 famous psychology studies — including ego depletion and the power-pose effect. Only ~36% replicated cleanly. What did the effort find?
answer: Many famous results failed — single studies are weaker than headlines suggest
choices: Many famous results failed — single studies are weaker than headlines suggest
Every famous result replicated — exactly as originally published
Famous results are unreplicable — by definition of being unique
Famous results were classified secret — and could not be retested
context: The 'replication crisis' anchored on Ioannidis's 2005 PLOS Medicine paper. Causes include p-hacking, publication bias, small samples, and outright fraud (Stapel, ~50 retractions). The field adopted pre-registration in response.

question: In 2005 epidemiologist John Ioannidis published a famous paper applying Bayesian reasoning to scientific publishing. What was the title and key claim?
answer: 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' — single studies are weak evidence
choices: 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' — single studies are weak evidence
'Why Every Scientific Paper Is Always Correct' — papers should be trusted absolutely
'Why Scientists Should Stop Publishing' — research should remain unpublished forever
'Why Public Funding Always Fails' — only private grants produce valid science
context: John Ioannidis (Stanford epidemiologist, born 1965) published 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' in PLOS Medicine in August 2005. He applied Bayesian reasoning about prior probabilities, study power, bias, and competition to show that — given typical practices — most published findings should be expected to be false. The paper has been cited tens of thousands of times. Ioannidis became one of the leading voices in the replication-crisis discussion, and was a notable Great Barrington Declaration signatory critical of pandemic lockdown policies.

question: In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley conducted a famous experiment trying to detect Earth's motion through a supposed medium called the 'luminiferous ether.' What did they find?
answer: No detectable motion through any ether, since the ether didn't exist
choices: No detectable motion through any ether, since the ether didn't exist
Earth moving at exactly the predicted speed through the ether
An ether wind so strong it nearly destroyed the apparatus
Multiple ethers each moving in different directions at the time
context: Michelson and Morley used a sensitive interferometer to compare light speeds in different directions. If Earth was moving through an ether, light should travel faster downstream than across. They found no difference at all — a 'null result.' The puzzle stood for nearly 20 years until Einstein's 1905 special relativity explained why: there is no ether, and the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of motion. The Michelson-Morley experiment is one of the most famous 'beautiful failures' in physics — the failure itself was the discovery.

question: Einstein's 1915 general relativity predicted gravity would bend starlight near the Sun. The 1919 total solar eclipse offered the first major test. Who led the confirming expedition?
answer: Arthur Eddington, who photographed stars near the eclipsed Sun from Príncipe
choices: Arthur Eddington, who photographed stars near the eclipsed Sun from Príncipe
Edwin Hubble, observing only from Mount Wilson in California
Albert Michelson, attempting another null result like 1887
Marie Curie, joining the expedition from Paris during the war
context: Arthur Eddington (1882-1944), a British astronomer and Quaker pacifist, led an expedition to the island of Príncipe (off West Africa) to photograph the total solar eclipse of May 29, 1919. A parallel expedition went to Sobral, Brazil. The photographs showed star positions shifted by about Einstein's predicted amount, vindicating general relativity over Newton. The November 1919 announcement made Einstein a global celebrity overnight. Modern reanalysis has questioned how confidently the 1919 data alone could distinguish the theories — but later confirmations are airtight.

question: Robert Millikan won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics for measuring the electric charge of a single electron. What experimental technique did he use?
answer: Watching tiny oil droplets fall and rise between charged plates
choices: Watching tiny oil droplets fall and rise between charged plates
Counting raindrops on a London window during one rainy day
Throwing magnets in the air to attract electrons from clouds
Heating water until electrons appeared in the steam visibly
context: Millikan's 1909 oil-drop experiment used an atomizer to spray microscopic oil droplets between two horizontal metal plates. By measuring how fast individual droplets fell under gravity and then adjusting the plate voltage to slow or reverse their fall, he calculated the charge on each droplet. He found all measured charges were integer multiples of a fundamental unit — the electron's charge, 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs. Subsequent reviews of Millikan's notebooks suggest he may have selectively reported data, but the measured value held up to later precise determinations.

question: Thomas Young's 1801 double-slit experiment provided strong evidence about the nature of light. What surprising result did he find?
answer: Light created interference patterns, behaving as a wave and not just particles
choices: Light created interference patterns, behaving as a wave and not just particles
Light disappeared entirely when passing through any two narrow slits
Light split into rainbow colors only at certain seasons of the year
Light only worked when shone through perfectly square openings
context: Young (1773-1829) shone light through two close-spaced parallel slits onto a screen. Instead of two bright spots (as expected if light was particles), he saw an interference pattern with alternating bright and dark bands — exactly what happens when waves overlap. His experiment overturned Newton's earlier 'corpuscular' theory of light as particles. In the 20th century, the same double-slit experiment performed with single electrons produced the same wave pattern — one of the strangest results in quantum physics. Light is both wave AND particle, depending on what you measure.

question: Johannes Kepler (1571-1630) published the rules that planets follow as they orbit the Sun. What was his most counter-intuitive finding about planetary orbits?
answer: Planets orbit in ellipses, not circles as believed for 2000 years
choices: Planets orbit in ellipses, not circles as believed for 2000 years
Planets orbit only on Tuesdays and stop at all other times
Planets are perfectly stationary and the Sun moves around them
Planets all orbit at the exact same speed regardless of their size
context: Kepler used Tycho Brahe's precise observations of Mars to discover that planets follow elliptical (oval) orbits with the Sun at one focus. This overturned the ancient Greek-and-medieval assumption that celestial bodies must move in perfect circles. Kepler's three laws (1609, 1619) became the empirical foundation Newton used to derive universal gravitation in 1687. Kepler also discovered that planets sweep out equal areas in equal times (faster when closer to the Sun) and that orbital period squared is proportional to semi-major axis cubed.

question: In 1909-1911 Ernest Rutherford and his students at Manchester directed alpha particles at thin gold foil. What surprising result reshaped the atomic model?
answer: A few particles bounced almost straight back, so atoms must have tiny dense nuclei
choices: A few particles bounced almost straight back, so atoms must have tiny dense nuclei
Every single particle passed straight through, suggesting atoms are entirely empty
Every particle stopped immediately, suggesting atoms are entirely solid all through
The gold foil ignited and burned brightly, confirming no atomic structure exists
context: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working in Rutherford's lab, observed that ~1 in 8000 alpha particles bounced backward — like a 15-inch shell bouncing off tissue paper. Rutherford's interpretation (1911): atoms aren't uniform 'plum puddings' (J.J. Thomson's earlier model). Almost all the mass is concentrated in a tiny dense nucleus at the center, with electrons orbiting at distance. This model was refined by Bohr (1913) and finally absorbed into quantum mechanics in the 1920s.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table grouped elements with similar chemical behavior in the same column. What did this organization eventually reveal about the underlying structure of atoms?
answer: Elements in the same column have similar outer-electron configurations
choices: Elements in the same column have similar outer-electron configurations
Elements in the same column are all liquids at room temperature
Elements in the same column all have exactly the same atomic weight
Elements in the same column come from the same star originally
context: Mendeleev grouped elements by chemical behavior in 1869 without knowing about electrons or atomic structure. We now know that elements in the same column share outer-electron (valence shell) configurations — which determines their chemistry. The noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn) all have full outer shells, making them chemically inert. The halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) all lack one electron, making them highly reactive. Atomic structure (Bohr 1913, Schrödinger 1926) eventually explained why Mendeleev's empirical pattern existed.

question: Before the 1860s most diseases were thought to be caused by 'miasma' (bad air) or imbalanced humors. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch overturned this view. What did they show diseases are actually caused by?
answer: Specific microorganisms, bacteria and other microbes invisible to the eye
choices: Specific microorganisms, bacteria and other microbes invisible to the eye
Bad luck and individual moral failings that cannot be measured
Curses placed on specific families by other people deliberately
Old age alone, with no other identifiable causes whatsoever
context: Germ theory developed through the work of many — Ignaz Semmelweis (hand-washing, 1847), Louis Pasteur (microbes cause fermentation and disease, 1860s), Joseph Lister (antiseptic surgery, 1860s), and Robert Koch (proving specific microbes cause specific diseases: anthrax 1876, tuberculosis 1882, cholera 1884). Koch's postulates established how to prove a particular microbe caused a particular disease. The germ theory transformed medicine: by 1900 once-deadly diseases (puerperal fever, surgical infection, cholera) had been substantially reduced where germ-theory hygiene was adopted.

question: James Watson's 1968 memoir 'The Double Helix' offered an unusually frank — and controversial — account of the DNA-structure discovery. What was particularly controversial about the book?
answer: Its dismissive treatment of Rosalind Franklin, criticized as ungenerous and sexist
choices: Its dismissive treatment of Rosalind Franklin, criticized as ungenerous and sexist
Its claim that Watson had personally discovered every step alone
Its claim that the structure was wrong and should be re-derived
Its claim that Crick had not actually been involved in any way
context: Watson's 'The Double Helix' (1968) was praised for its candor about the messiness of real science but harshly criticized for its treatment of Rosalind Franklin. Watson described her as obstructive and intellectually limited, with frequent comments on her appearance and clothing. Crick and others pushed back. Aaron Klug (Franklin's colleague) and Anne Sayre's biography 'Rosalind Franklin and DNA' (1975) corrected the record. Watson himself later expressed some regret over the framing. Subsequent histories give Franklin substantial credit for the structural insights, though Nobel rules excluded her posthumously.

question: After the Permian-Triassic 'Great Dying' extinction wiped out ~90% of marine species, how long did Earth's biosphere take to recover its previous diversity?
answer: About 10 million years, with marine reefs gone the whole time
choices: About 10 million years, with marine reefs gone the whole time
About 100 years, with recovery complete by the next century
About 1,000 years, completing in a single millennium
About 1 billion years, with recovery still ongoing today
context: The Permian-Triassic extinction (252 million years ago) so devastated Earth's ecosystems that recovery took roughly 10 million years. Marine reefs essentially disappeared and didn't reform for 10 million years. On land, the 'coal gap' of the early Triassic shows almost no plant deposits — forests took as long to recover. The new biota that emerged was dominated by archosaurs (eventually leading to dinosaurs and modern crocodilians). The Great Dying reshaped which lineages would dominate Earth for the next ~180 million years.

question: In 1925 a young Tennessee high school teacher named John Scopes was put on trial for teaching evolution, violating the state's recent Butler Act. What was the outcome of the trial?
answer: Scopes was convicted and fined $100, with the verdict later overturned on a technicality
choices: Scopes was convicted and fined $100, with the verdict later overturned on a technicality
Scopes was acquitted unanimously by the jury after one day of testimony
Scopes won a million dollars in damages from the State of Tennessee
Scopes died during the trial and the proceedings were canceled outright
context: John Scopes (1900-1970) was a substitute teacher who agreed to be the test case after the ACLU offered to defend any teacher charged under Tennessee's 1925 Butler Act (banning teaching of evolution in public schools). Clarence Darrow defended Scopes; William Jennings Bryan led the prosecution. The trial became a national spectacle. Scopes was convicted and fined $100. The Tennessee Supreme Court overturned on a technicality (the fine had been set by judge not jury). The Butler Act remained on Tennessee books until 1967.

question: The 'Big Bang' theory of cosmic origins was first proposed in 1927 by a scientist who was also a Catholic priest. Who was he, and what did he call his original idea?
answer: Georges Lemaître, who called it the 'primeval atom' hypothesis
choices: Georges Lemaître, who called it the 'primeval atom' hypothesis
Edwin Hubble, calling it the 'expanding universe' idea
Albert Einstein, calling it the 'cosmological constant' problem
Gregor Mendel, calling it the 'inheritance of cosmic matter' theory
context: Father Georges Lemaître (1894-1966), Belgian priest and physicist, proposed in 1927 that the universe began as a single 'primeval atom' that expanded outward. The idea was initially controversial (some accused him of importing Genesis into physics). Edwin Hubble's 1929 observations of galaxy redshifts supported expansion. The name 'Big Bang' was coined sarcastically by Fred Hoyle in 1949 — Hoyle preferred the rival 'Steady State' theory. Pope Pius XII embraced the Big Bang in 1951; Lemaître asked the Pope to stop, arguing science and theology should stay separate.

question: Tycho Brahe (1546-1601), a Danish nobleman, built the most accurate naked-eye astronomical observatory in history at Uraniborg on the island of Hven. Why did his observations turn out to be so important?
answer: They were precise enough for Kepler to derive the laws of planetary motion
choices: They were precise enough for Kepler to derive the laws of planetary motion
They proved the Earth-centered model of the universe definitively
They predicted the exact date of every solar eclipse for the next thousand years
They discovered the existence of all eight planets of our solar system
context: Tycho Brahe's observations of planetary positions were accurate to about 1 arcminute — astonishing for naked-eye instruments. He had a famously colorful life: a metal nose (lost in a youthful duel), a pet elk that died after drinking too much beer, and a private island given to him by the Danish king. After his death (1601), his assistant Johannes Kepler inherited his data. Kepler's analysis of Tycho's Mars observations led to the discovery that planets follow elliptical orbits — the foundation Newton would build on.

question: When Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid in 1865, British surgeons resisted his techniques for years. What links this resistance to other cases like Semmelweis and Wegener?
answer: Established practitioners often resist methods that challenge their training
choices: Established practitioners often resist methods that challenge their training
British surgeons accepted Lister's methods immediately and unanimously
Lister abandoned his methods after British surgeons rejected them all
Lister's methods were endorsed by Parliament before any clinical trial
context: Lister published his results in 1867 in The Lancet — post-surgical infection rates dropped dramatically using carbolic acid. British surgeons were skeptical (Lister was Scottish and at Glasgow, not the London establishment); they doubted germ theory and were proud of their existing techniques (the 'good old surgical stink' was sometimes worn as a badge of honor). American surgeons adopted Listerism more quickly. The Semmelweis-Lister-Marshall pattern shows that mid-career practitioners can be the most resistant to evidence — a recurring obstacle in medical reform.

question: Historians sometimes use the term 'Scientific Revolution' for a roughly two-century period when modern science emerged. What dates do most historians bracket the Scientific Revolution between?
answer: Roughly 1543 (Copernicus) to 1687 (Newton's Principia)
choices: Roughly 1543 (Copernicus) to 1687 (Newton's Principia)
Roughly 1066 (Norman Conquest) to 1500 (early Renaissance only)
Roughly 1800 (Industrial Revolution) to 2000 (modern science only)
Roughly 700 BC (Greek philosophy) to 1500 AD (Renaissance start)
context: The 'Scientific Revolution' is conventionally bracketed by Copernicus's 'On the Revolutions' (1543) and Newton's 'Principia' (1687). Major moments: Copernicus's heliocentrism (1543); Vesalius's anatomy (1543); Galileo's telescope (1609) and trial (1633); Kepler's laws (1609, 1619); Harvey on blood circulation (1628); Royal Society founded (1660); Newton's optics (1672) and Principia (1687). The period saw the emergence of experimental method, mathematical natural philosophy, and the institutions (academies, journals, peer review) that we still use today.

question: One of the world's oldest scientific societies was founded in London in 1660 and still operates today. What is it called?
answer: The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge
choices: The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge
The American Academy of Sciences, founded that year by colonists
The Vatican Pontifical Academy, founded in the year 1666 in Rome
The Russian Academy, founded by Peter the Great in St. Petersburg
context: The Royal Society was founded November 28, 1660 by 12 men who included Robert Boyle, Christopher Wren, and John Wilkins. King Charles II granted a royal charter in 1662. The society's motto 'Nullius in verba' ('take no one's word for it') captures its founding spirit: empirical evidence, not appeal to authority. Members have included Newton, Darwin, Maxwell, Rutherford, Curie, Einstein, Crick, Watson, and Hawking. The Society's 'Philosophical Transactions' (founded 1665) is one of the longest-running scientific journals in the world.

question: Trofim Lysenko was a Soviet agronomist who dominated Russian biology from the 1930s through 1965. The Soviet state backed his ideas while suppressing real genetics. What is the broader lesson of his career?
answer: Politically-favored science can suppress real biology for decades
choices: Politically-favored science can suppress real biology for decades
Politically-favored science always agrees with real biology
Lysenko was correct and Western biology is still wrong on genes
The Soviet government had no influence on which ideas prevailed
context: Trofim Lysenko (1898-1976) rejected Mendelian genetics in favor of a Lamarckian view that organisms could pass on acquired traits. Stalin and Khrushchev backed him; geneticists who disagreed were dismissed, imprisoned, or executed (Nikolai Vavilov, the great seed-bank founder, died in prison in 1943). Soviet agriculture suffered famines partly from Lysenko's failed crop programs. Lysenkoism dominated until 1965. The episode is the clearest 20th-century case of political ideology imposed onto biology — and a warning about the cost of suppressing scientific dissent.

question: Johannes Kepler spent years grinding through Tycho Brahe's planetary observations. He found that planets sweep out equal areas in equal times. What's the physical meaning of that 'second law'?
answer: Planets move faster when nearer the Sun and slower when farther — speed adjusts with distance
choices: Planets move faster when nearer the Sun and slower when farther — speed adjusts with distance
Planets move at exactly the same speed for the entire orbit — a perfect circle was always assumed
Planets pause briefly at the farthest point — gravity 'resets' before pulling them back inward
Planets reverse direction once per orbit — the sweep-equal-areas idea required backward motion
context: Kepler's three laws (1609 and 1619) replaced the perfect-circle Greek picture with elliptical orbits. The second law follows from conservation of angular momentum, which Newton later derived from gravity. Brahe had the data; Kepler had the patience to fit ellipses through it.

question: Kepler's first law overturned a 2,000-year-old assumption from Aristotle and Ptolemy. What was that assumption, and what did Kepler replace it with?
answer: Planets travel in perfect circles — Kepler showed orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus
choices: Planets travel in perfect circles — Kepler showed orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Planets travel through crystalline spheres — Kepler showed orbits are powered by angelic guidance
Planets do not move at all — Kepler showed the stars and Sun travel around an immobile Earth
Planets travel in spirals — Kepler showed orbits gradually drift outward over centuries of time
context: From Pythagoras through Ptolemy, the circle was treated as the only motion 'worthy' of the heavens. Kepler's ellipses (1609) broke that aesthetic stranglehold. Copernicus had already moved the Sun to the center but kept the circles.

question: Kepler's third law connects two simple quantities for any planet: the period (T) and the average distance from the Sun (a). What's the relationship?
answer: T squared is proportional to a cubed — farther planets take disproportionately longer to orbit
choices: T squared is proportional to a cubed — farther planets take disproportionately longer to orbit
T equals a — distance from the Sun in AU equals period in years for every planet exactly
T is proportional to a — Mars is 1.5x farther than Earth, so Mars takes 1.5 Earth years
T squared is proportional to a — Jupiter would take only about 5 Earth years to orbit once
context: T^2 / a^3 is the same constant for every planet around the Sun. Earth (T=1 yr, a=1 AU) gives 1. Newton later derived the law from F=GMm/r^2 and centripetal motion, vindicating Kepler.

question: James Clerk Maxwell's 1865 equations united three things people had treated as separate phenomena. Which three did Maxwell show were one connected thing?
answer: Electricity, magnetism, and light — light is an electromagnetic wave
choices: Electricity, magnetism, and light — light is an electromagnetic wave
Heat, gravity, and electricity — heat and gravity move charges through metals
Sound, magnetism, and gravity — pressure waves bend magnetic field lines
Magnetism, gravity, and chemistry — molecular bonds were shown to be magnetic forces
context: Maxwell's equations predicted electromagnetic waves traveling at exactly the speed of light. Heinrich Hertz produced radio waves in 1888, confirming the prediction. Einstein later called Maxwell's work 'the most profound and the most fruitful' physics had ever undergone.

question: Maxwell's equations predicted that electromagnetic waves should travel through a vacuum at a specific speed — and the number matched a quantity already measured. Which measured quantity matched?
answer: The speed of light — about 300,000 km/s, already measured by Fizeau and Foucault before Maxwell
choices: The speed of light — about 300,000 km/s, already measured by Fizeau and Foucault before Maxwell
The speed of sound — about 340 m/s, measured in the air at sea-level temperature
The speed of Earth's rotation — about 1,670 km/h at the equator, well known to navigators
The orbital speed of Mercury — about 47 km/s, measured by Le Verrier in the same decade
context: Fizeau (1849) and Foucault (1862) had measured light's speed using rotating mirrors and toothed wheels. Maxwell's prediction that EM waves traveled at this exact speed unified optics with electromagnetism — among the great theoretical achievements of the 19th century.

question: A spinning ice skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. No outside force pushes her — yet her rotation speed increases. What conservation law explains this?
answer: Conservation of angular momentum — arms-in reduces moment of inertia, so spin rate rises
choices: Conservation of angular momentum — arms-in reduces moment of inertia, so spin rate rises
Conservation of energy — pulling arms in releases stored potential energy as faster motion
Conservation of mass — arms-in concentrates the skater's mass, which speeds up rotation
Conservation of charge — the skater's body builds up static charge, which accelerates her spin
context: Angular momentum L = I*omega is conserved when no external torque acts. Pulling arms in decreases I (moment of inertia), so omega (spin rate) must increase to keep L constant. The same principle controls how neutron stars spin so fast after collapse.

question: A pendulum at the top of its swing has lots of potential energy and almost no kinetic energy. At the bottom, it's reversed. What broader physics principle does this swap illustrate?
answer: Energy is conserved — kinetic and potential energy interchange, the total stays the same in an ideal swing
choices: Energy is conserved — kinetic and potential energy interchange, the total stays the same in an ideal swing
Energy is destroyed — at the bottom, gravity 'absorbs' all the energy and the pendulum eventually stops
Energy is created — the swinging motion generates new energy from the Earth's magnetic field
Energy comes from heat — the friction at the pivot point converts thermal energy into motion
context: Conservation of energy is one of physics' deepest principles. Real pendulums slow because of friction and air resistance — that energy doesn't vanish, it becomes heat. Emmy Noether proved in 1918 that every conservation law corresponds to a symmetry.

question: Emmy Noether published a theorem in 1918 linking conservation laws to symmetries of nature. What does her theorem connect to conservation of energy?
answer: Time-translation symmetry — physics works the same today as yesterday, so energy is conserved
choices: Time-translation symmetry — physics works the same today as yesterday, so energy is conserved
Spatial reflection symmetry — physics looks the same in a mirror, so energy must be conserved
Charge-conjugation symmetry — swapping positive and negative charges preserves total energy
Color symmetry — quarks can swap color labels without changing total energy of the system
context: Noether's theorem: every continuous symmetry implies a conservation law. Time-translation symmetry implies energy conservation. Space-translation implies momentum conservation. Rotational symmetry implies angular momentum conservation. Einstein called Noether the most important woman in mathematics.

question: In 1905, while working as a patent clerk in Bern, the 26-year-old Albert Einstein published four papers in one year. Which collective name do physicists use for his 1905 output?
answer: Annus mirabilis — Latin for 'miracle year', each paper reshaped a field of physics
choices: Annus mirabilis — Latin for 'miracle year', each paper reshaped a field of physics
Annus horribilis — Latin for 'terrible year', the papers were widely rejected at the time
Annus magnus — Latin for 'great year', all four papers used calculus invented by Newton
Annus solaris — Latin for 'solar year', the papers focused on energy from the Sun
context: The 1905 papers covered the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and mass-energy equivalence (E=mc^2). Einstein was 26, working at the Swiss Patent Office. He won the 1921 Nobel for the photoelectric paper — not for relativity, which the committee considered too controversial.

question: Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion explained why tiny pollen grains under a microscope jiggle around in water. What did Einstein argue was causing the jiggling?
answer: Random collisions with invisible water molecules — strong evidence atoms were real
choices: Random collisions with invisible water molecules — strong evidence atoms were real
Tiny electrical currents in the pollen — proving life had its own kind of magnetism
Heat radiating up from the microscope lamp — moving the grains by warming the water
Magnetic forces from Earth's field — pulling pollen grains in unpredictable directions
context: Botanist Robert Brown had observed the jiggle in 1827. Einstein's 1905 paper gave a quantitative theory: molecules bombarding the grain from all sides, with statistical fluctuations producing the visible motion. Jean Perrin's 1908 experiments confirmed the predictions, finally settling the atomic-theory debate.

question: Einstein's most famous equation, E = mc^2, was published in a short follow-up paper in 1905. What does it say about mass and energy?
answer: Mass and energy are interchangeable — a small mass equals a huge amount of energy
choices: Mass and energy are interchangeable — a small mass equals a huge amount of energy
Mass and energy are independent — they happen to share equations but not substance
Mass is created by energy — every collision adds extra atomic mass to the participants
Energy destroys mass — the more energy you add, the lighter an object eventually becomes
context: Because c (the speed of light) is huge — about 3*10^8 m/s — squaring it gives 9*10^16. So 1 kg of mass equals 9*10^16 joules. This is why nuclear reactions (fission, fusion) release so much energy from tiny mass differences. Atomic bombs and stars exploit this.

question: Einstein's 1905 photoelectric paper explained why light shining on a metal can knock electrons loose. What was the surprising claim that won him the 1921 Nobel?
answer: Light comes in discrete packets (photons) whose energy depends on frequency — not just brightness
choices: Light comes in discrete packets (photons) whose energy depends on frequency — not just brightness
Light is always a continuous wave — electrons only escape if total wave energy crosses a threshold
Light carries no energy at all — heated metals release electrons regardless of any light shining
Light slows electrons down — the photoelectric effect was an artifact of dirty experimental setups
context: Classical wave theory predicted brighter light should always free electrons. Experiments showed only sufficient FREQUENCY mattered — dim violet light freed electrons, bright red light didn't. Einstein's quantum explanation broke from classical physics. Robert Millikan confirmed it experimentally by 1916, despite hoping to disprove it.

question: Einstein's special relativity (1905) is built on two postulates. The first: physics looks the same in every non-accelerating frame. What's the famously counter-intuitive second postulate?
answer: The speed of light in vacuum is the same for every observer — regardless of their own motion
choices: The speed of light in vacuum is the same for every observer — regardless of their own motion
Time runs at the same rate for every observer — clocks always tick together if synchronized once
Space and time are independent quantities — they cannot be combined into a single quantity
All bodies attract each other with equal force — gravity is the only universal interaction
context: The constancy of light's speed forces time and space to bend instead. Time dilation (moving clocks run slow), length contraction (moving objects shrink along their motion), and mass-energy equivalence all follow. Confirmed countless times — GPS satellites must correct for it to stay accurate.

question: An astronaut leaves Earth at near light-speed, travels to a star, and returns. When she steps off the ship, less time has passed for her than for her twin on Earth. What's this prediction called?
answer: The twin paradox — special relativity says moving clocks run slow
choices: The twin paradox — special relativity says moving clocks run slow
The dark-twin paradox — light could not have made the same trip the astronaut did
The Newton paradox — classical mechanics could not predict the time difference
The grandfather paradox — visiting the past would erase the astronaut's own birth
context: Time dilation is real and measured. Muons from cosmic rays survive Earth-impact only because their internal clocks tick slowly in our frame. Atomic clocks flown around the world (Hafele-Keating, 1971) returned reading slightly less than ground clocks, exactly as predicted.

question: In Newton's physics, simultaneity is absolute — two events either happen at the same time or they don't, period. Einstein showed that even simultaneity is what?
answer: Frame-dependent — two events simultaneous for one observer aren't simultaneous for another moving observer
choices: Frame-dependent — two events simultaneous for one observer aren't simultaneous for another moving observer
Imaginary — events never actually happen at the same time in any real situation
Magnetic — only events involving the same magnetic field can be simultaneous
Random — quantum mechanics forbids two distant events from being simultaneous
context: If light travels at the same speed for everyone, observers in relative motion disagree about which events happen 'at the same time.' The classic thought experiment: lightning hits both ends of a moving train. The stationary platform observer sees them simultaneously; the train passenger doesn't.

question: Max Planck in 1900 proposed that energy from a hot object isn't released continuously but in tiny discrete chunks. What did he call these chunks?
answer: Quanta — Latin for 'how much', the seed concept behind all of quantum mechanics
choices: Quanta — Latin for 'how much', the seed concept behind all of quantum mechanics
Atoms — the same word used by ancient Greeks for indivisible bits of matter
Photons — particles of light, a term coined later by Gilbert Lewis in 1926
Waves — packets of regular wave-energy, not separate from classical light theory
context: Planck introduced quanta to fix the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' in blackbody radiation. He thought of it as a mathematical trick at first. Einstein took the idea seriously in 1905 with photons. Bohr applied it to atomic orbits in 1913. The quantum revolution had begun.

question: Niels Bohr's 1913 model of the atom imagined electrons traveling around the nucleus in specific allowed orbits — they couldn't be anywhere they wanted. What did Bohr's model explain that earlier ones couldn't?
answer: The discrete colors of light hydrogen emits when heated — each color was a jump between orbits
choices: The discrete colors of light hydrogen emits when heated — each color was a jump between orbits
Why atoms had any color at all — earlier models predicted all atoms should look identical
Why electrons existed in pairs — Bohr predicted spin a full decade before its discovery
Why some atoms were radioactive — only atoms with electron mismatches could decay
context: Hydrogen heated in a tube emits specific wavelengths (the Balmer series, etc.) — sharp lines, not a continuous rainbow. Bohr's quantized orbits explained why: electrons jumping between specific energy levels emit photons of specific frequencies. The picture was later refined by Schrodinger and Heisenberg, but Bohr's leap was the key.

question: Erwin Schrodinger's 1926 wave equation gave a new way to describe electrons in atoms. What replaced Bohr's picture of electrons on definite orbits?
answer: Probability clouds — regions where the electron is likely to be found, not specific paths
choices: Probability clouds — regions where the electron is likely to be found, not specific paths
Crystal lattices — fixed positions inside microscopic geometric shapes inside atoms
Tiny spheres — electrons as solid balls bouncing between proton walls in the nucleus
Magnetic fields — the electron itself dissolved into a pure rotating field of force
context: Schrodinger's equation describes the wavefunction (psi), whose squared magnitude gives the probability of finding the electron at each location. The electron has no definite position until measured. This was a radical departure from classical determinism and remains the foundation of chemistry and modern physics.

question: Thomas Young in 1801 shone light through two narrow parallel slits and watched the pattern on a screen behind. What did he see that proved something important about light?
answer: Bright and dark stripes — an interference pattern, showing light behaves like a wave
choices: Bright and dark stripes — an interference pattern, showing light behaves like a wave
Two sharp bright spots — exactly what you'd expect if light traveled as solid particles
A single bright glow — light scattered uniformly, with no detectable pattern at all
Concentric rings — light reflected back into shapes resembling raindrop ripples in a pond
context: Two-slit interference is the hallmark of waves: peaks reinforce (bright) where two waves arrive in phase; cancel (dark) where they arrive out of phase. Young's experiment overturned Newton's particle theory of light — for a century. Then 1905 reopened it.

question: If you fire SINGLE photons one at a time through Young's two-slit setup, they still build up an interference pattern over time. What does this seem to imply about each individual photon?
answer: Each photon passes through both slits at once — and interferes with itself
choices: Each photon passes through both slits at once — and interferes with itself
Each photon picks one slit at random — the pattern is a statistical illusion
Each photon splits at the slits — and rejoins on the way to the screen
The detector itself creates the pattern — single photons travel as straight lines
context: Single-photon double-slit experiments (first done with electrons by Tonomura's team, 1989, also with photons and molecules) show wave-particle duality directly. The photon's wavefunction passes through both slits; measurement at the screen 'collapses' it to one spot. This is the heart of quantum weirdness.

question: In the double-slit setup, if you add a detector at one slit that tells you which slit each photon went through, the interference pattern disappears. What does this tell us about measurement in quantum mechanics?
answer: Observing which slit collapses the wavefunction — the act of measurement changes the system
choices: Observing which slit collapses the wavefunction — the act of measurement changes the system
Detectors emit waves that cancel the pattern — pure interference still occurs unobserved
Photons accelerate near detectors — they punch through slits too fast for interference
Interference vanishes randomly — measurement at slits has no effect on the screen pattern
context: The 'which-path' experiments are real, not thought-experiment. Getting which-slit information — by any means — destroys the interference pattern. This is the 'measurement problem' at the heart of quantum mechanics. Different interpretations (Copenhagen, many-worlds, pilot-wave) try to make sense of it.

question: Werner Heisenberg's 1927 uncertainty principle says you cannot simultaneously know both a particle's position and its momentum with perfect precision. What's the deeper point of this principle?
answer: It's not a measurement limit — it's built into nature itself; precise position has no precise momentum
choices: It's not a measurement limit — it's built into nature itself; precise position has no precise momentum
It's purely a measurement limit — better instruments would eventually measure both perfectly
It applies only to electrons — protons and neutrons have definite position and momentum
It vanishes at low speeds — uncertainty is a relativistic effect that disappears at human scales
context: Position-momentum uncertainty is a feature of the wavefunction itself, not a measurement artifact. Heisenberg showed Delta(x) * Delta(p) >= h-bar/2. Energy-time uncertainty also exists. The principle restricts classical determinism — even with perfect instruments, the future cannot be precisely predicted.

question: In Heisenberg's picture, can you observe an electron without disturbing it?
answer: No — every measurement requires interaction (a photon, an electron probe) that changes the system
choices: No — every measurement requires interaction (a photon, an electron probe) that changes the system
Yes — modern instruments are non-interacting and reveal electrons without any change
Sometimes — only on Tuesdays, when the magnetic field of the Earth is at its minimum
Only in a vacuum — air molecules normally interfere, but a vacuum chamber removes that issue
context: Quantum measurement is inseparable from the system measured. To 'see' an electron's position you need a photon, which gives it a momentum kick. This is one reason the Copenhagen interpretation says quantum systems do not have definite properties until measured.

question: Belgian Catholic priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre in 1927 proposed that the universe began from a single dense state and has been expanding since. What did the Cambridge astronomer Fred Hoyle later sarcastically call it?
answer: 'The Big Bang' — Hoyle disliked the theory but coined its now-universal nickname
choices: 'The Big Bang' — Hoyle disliked the theory but coined its now-universal nickname
'The Cosmic Pop' — a phrase he used in private letters, never on the BBC
'The Singular Snap' — Hoyle's preferred technical term, abandoned by other astronomers
'The Hot Beginning' — Hoyle's accepted alternative, widely adopted in journals
context: Lemaitre called it the 'primeval atom' or the 'cosmic egg.' Hoyle, who championed the rival steady-state theory, coined 'Big Bang' on BBC radio in 1949 as dismissive shorthand. The name stuck even as Hoyle's own theory lost to the evidence (CMB, abundance of light elements).

question: When astronomers say the universe is about 13.8 billion years old, where does that specific number come from?
answer: Measurements of cosmic expansion rate combined with the cosmic microwave background data
choices: Measurements of cosmic expansion rate combined with the cosmic microwave background data
Counting the number of stars in the Milky Way and dividing by their average lifetime
The age of the oldest meteorites found on Earth, since they formed shortly after the Big Bang
Carbon-14 dating of the most distant galaxies visible through the Hubble Space Telescope
context: The age comes from running the expansion backward (using the Hubble constant) and from fits to the cosmic microwave background's tiny variations (Planck satellite, etc.). The 13.8 Gyr figure has standard-model error bars of about 1%. There's tension between local and CMB-based measurements that may eventually require new physics.

question: In the early universe, before atoms could form, what did the cosmos look like? Pick the best plain-English description.
answer: A hot, dense plasma of charged particles — light couldn't travel far before scattering
choices: A hot, dense plasma of charged particles — light couldn't travel far before scattering
A cold, empty void — particles existed but were too far apart to interact at all
A solid block of matter — every cubic centimeter was packed with iron-like material
A black hole at every point — gravity was so strong nothing could escape anywhere
context: For about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe was opaque — free electrons scattered photons constantly, like fog scatters light. When the cosmos cooled enough for neutral atoms to form ('recombination'), photons could travel freely. Those freed photons are now the cosmic microwave background.

question: Edwin Hubble's 1929 paper from Mount Wilson Observatory established something that overturned the picture of a static cosmos. What did Hubble's redshift measurements show?
answer: Galaxies are moving away from us — the farther a galaxy is, the faster it's receding
choices: Galaxies are moving away from us — the farther a galaxy is, the faster it's receding
Galaxies stay where they are — redshifts are caused by the chemistry of distant stars
Galaxies are moving toward us — the Milky Way sits at the center of cosmic gravity
Galaxies are random — half move toward us, half away, with no pattern by distance
context: Hubble built on earlier work by Vesto Slipher and Lemaitre. His galaxy-velocity vs. distance plot showed a roughly linear relation: v = H_0 * d. This was the first observational evidence for cosmic expansion. The Hubble constant H_0 measures today's expansion rate. Einstein had abandoned his 'static universe' fudge by 1931.

question: When astronomers say a distant galaxy is 'redshifted', what does that physically mean?
answer: Its light is stretched to longer (redder) wavelengths — the galaxy is moving away from us
choices: Its light is stretched to longer (redder) wavelengths — the galaxy is moving away from us
Its light passes through red dust on the way to us — filters made the galaxy look red
Its stars are old red giants — there are no young blue stars in the galaxy's structure
Its light is reflected by the Sun's atmosphere — Earth's atmosphere makes everything redder
context: Redshift is a Doppler-like effect for light: moving-away sources have wavelengths shifted toward red; moving-toward sources are blueshifted. In cosmology, redshift comes from the expansion of space itself, not just relative motion. Quantitatively: 1+z = a_now / a_then, where a is the cosmic scale factor.

question: American astronomer Vera Rubin in the 1970s measured how fast stars orbit at the outer edges of galaxies. What did she find that earlier theory couldn't explain?
answer: Outer stars orbit much faster than visible-mass gravity predicts — suggesting unseen mass
choices: Outer stars orbit much faster than visible-mass gravity predicts — suggesting unseen mass
Outer stars don't orbit at all — they drift freely in the empty space between galaxies
Outer stars orbit at random — no consistent pattern across different galaxies was found
Outer stars only emit infrared light — they showed no orbital motion in optical telescopes
context: Newtonian gravity says outer stars should orbit slower (like outer planets in our solar system). Rubin found flat rotation curves — outer stars orbit at roughly the same high speed as inner stars. That implies far more mass than we can see — what we now call dark matter. Rubin never received a Nobel; she died in 2016.

question: Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe's mass-energy by current estimates, but no direct detection has succeeded. What's the most honest answer about what dark matter actually IS?
answer: We don't know — many candidate particles have been proposed; none has been confirmed
choices: We don't know — many candidate particles have been proposed; none has been confirmed
We know it's regular hydrogen gas — just very cold and hard to see with telescopes
We know it's neutrinos — confirmed by the IceCube South Pole observatory in 2018
It's a known particle — Higgs bosons fill the 'dark' mass gap precisely as expected
context: WIMPs, axions, sterile neutrinos, primordial black holes have all been proposed. Underground detectors (LUX, XENON, etc.) have set increasingly tight limits without seeing a signal. Some physicists prefer modified gravity (MOND) as an alternative. As of the mid-2020s, dark matter remains a genuine open mystery in physics.

question: Some physicists prefer an alternative explanation to dark matter called MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics). What does MOND propose, in plain English?
answer: Gravity itself works differently at very low accelerations — no missing mass needed
choices: Gravity itself works differently at very low accelerations — no missing mass needed
Galaxies are illusions — the rotation curves are artifacts of distant gravitational lensing
All stars are double — hidden binary companions add the 'missing' mass exactly
The Milky Way is much closer than thought — distance estimates inflate orbital speeds
context: Mordehai Milgrom proposed MOND in 1983. It fits galaxy rotation curves with no dark matter. It struggles with galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background, where dark matter fits well. The debate is unresolved — most cosmologists prefer dark matter, but MOND has serious defenders.

question: On May 29, 1919, Arthur Eddington led an expedition to photograph a total solar eclipse. He was testing a specific prediction of Einstein's 1915 general relativity. What did Einstein predict?
answer: Light from distant stars would bend as it passed near the Sun — by a measurable amount
choices: Light from distant stars would bend as it passed near the Sun — by a measurable amount
The Sun's mass would shrink during the eclipse — making it harder to see
The Moon would appear blue during the eclipse — Einstein had predicted this in 1916
Time would stop briefly during totality — clocks at the eclipse path would pause
context: Einstein predicted starlight would bend by about 1.75 arcseconds passing the Sun's edge — twice Newton's prediction. Eddington's eclipse photographs confirmed the prediction (within uncertainty). The Times of London headline: 'REVOLUTION IN SCIENCE — NEW THEORY OF THE UNIVERSE — NEWTONIAN IDEAS OVERTHROWN.' Einstein became a global celebrity overnight.

question: Modern reanalysis of Eddington's 1919 eclipse plates has questioned how confidently the original data alone supported Einstein over Newton. But why is Einstein's prediction now considered confirmed beyond doubt?
answer: Many later measurements — radio observations of quasars, GPS effects, gravitational waves — all confirm it
choices: Many later measurements — radio observations of quasars, GPS effects, gravitational waves — all confirm it
Eddington personally re-verified his data in 1940 — no later measurements were ever attempted
It was confirmed by 1922 by a German team — and never measured again afterward
It has never been confirmed — modern physicists are still arguing about Einstein's prediction
context: Radio-telescope observations of quasars passing near the Sun (from the 1960s onward) confirmed Einstein's deflection to within 0.1%. The GPS system requires general-relativity corrections to function. Gravitational waves (LIGO 2015) further confirmed it. Eddington's plates were just the start of a now-overwhelming evidence base.

question: Drop an ice cube in warm water and it always melts. Watch ANY video of melting ice in reverse and you can tell it's reversed instantly. What physical principle distinguishes 'forward' from 'backward' in time?
answer: The second law of thermodynamics — entropy of an isolated system tends to increase
choices: The second law of thermodynamics — entropy of an isolated system tends to increase
The conservation of energy — energy flows only forward through time, never backward
Newton's third law — every reaction has an opposite reaction, ordered in time
Einstein's E=mc^2 — mass-energy decreases over time, marking time's direction
context: Most physics laws are time-symmetric — they look the same run backwards. But the second law isn't. Disorder (entropy) almost always increases. This 'arrow of time' connects to thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, and ultimately cosmology — the early universe must have started in an extremely low-entropy state.
